$comment: Catalogue of test video sources for the media-infra stream harness.
No media is committed to this repository. Every source is fetched on demand
into test-streams/media/ (gitignored) and normalised into a DJI-like H.264
The drone-* sources are royalty-free stock clips from https://dronestock.com/
delivered over Mux. Royalty-free covers use, not redistribution of the raw
asset, so 'redistributable' is false for them: fetch locally, never commit or
Why real drone footage matters here: DJI aircraft push H.264 over RTMP with a
fixed GOP and no B-frames. Aerial motion (continuous translation across a
detailed ground plane) produces very different rate-control behaviour from
synthetic animation, so these clips exercise the encoder and the transport
far more like production traffic than a cartoon does.
Encoder profiles approximating DJI livestream quality tiers. All profiles
share GOP length, audio codec, sample rate and channel layout so that any
two assets built at the same profile stay concat-compatible, which is what
lets publish.sh chain a playlist with -c copy.

dji-hd.description: DJI 'HD' tier. Closest match to Pilot 2 / Dock default livestream.

dji-sd.description: DJI 'SD' tier. Typical of a constrained 4G uplink.

dji-smooth.description: DJI 'Smooth' tier. Worst-case uplink, useful for stress tests.

sources.$comment: Keys are the identifiers passed to fetch.sh and publish.sh.

drone-night-city.description: Aerial night flight over a city. Default source: low-light encoder stress.
drone-night-city.licence: Royalty-free stock clip from https://dronestock.com/ (delivered via Mux). Free to use; redistribution of the raw asset is not granted.
notes: Night urban scene: many small point lights over large dark areas, which is one of the harder cases for a rate-limited H.264 encoder.
29.97fps rather than 30, so normalising duplicates roughly one frame per second. Irrelevant for transport testing.
~17 MiB fetch for the top rendition, a couple of seconds on a decent link.

drone-winter-town.description: Daylight aerial over a snowy mill town. High spatial detail at 59.94fps.
drone-winter-town.licence: Royalty-free stock clip from https://dronestock.com/ (delivered via Mux). Free to use; redistribution of the raw asset is not granted.
notes: Complements drone-night-city: overcast daylight with very fine texture (snow, bare trees, parked cars) instead of low-light noise.
59.94fps source. Normalising to 30fps drops every second frame, which is exactly what a drone does when its uplink tier caps frame rate.
~14 MiB fetch for the top rendition.

drone-city-rooftops.description: Sunny daylight aerial over a dense European city. Cinemascope crop at 23.976fps.
drone-city-rooftops.licence: Royalty-free stock clip from https://dronestock.com/ (delivered via Mux). Free to use; redistribution of the raw asset is not granted.
notes: Terracotta rooftops, rail cuttings and tree canopy in bright sun: high-contrast, high-detail daylight.
The only non-16:9 source here (1920x1012, roughly 1.9:1). fetch.sh letterboxes it to the profile's frame rather than stretching it, so expect black bars top and bottom.
23.976fps. Normalising to 30fps duplicates frames unevenly; fine for transport, not for judging motion cadence.

drone-arid-coast.description: Aerial over a remote arid coastline with breaking surf. Large flat areas, moving water.
drone-arid-coast.licence: Royalty-free stock clip from https://dronestock.com/ (delivered via Mux). Free to use; redistribution of the raw asset is not granted.
notes: The opposite rate-control case to the city clips: most of the frame is low-detail sand, sky and open water, but the surf never stops moving.
Useful for spotting bitrate starvation artefacts, since a CBR encoder has spare bits here and should look clean.
Longest clip in the catalogue at 31s, so it is the best single source for a soak test.

bbb.description: Big Buck Bunny 1080p, 10s. Clearly licensed fallback for when redistribution matters.
notes: Synthetic animation, so its motion and rate-control behaviour are unlike real aerial footage. Use it when you need a source whose licence permits redistribution, or when offline.
The only source here that is safe to reference from CI.
